directAnswer: Pope Eugene IV was Gabriele Condulmer of Venice, a nephew of Gregory XII, who reigned from 3 March 1431 to 23 February 1447. His long struggle with the Council of Basel ended with his transfer of the council to Ferrara and Florence, where union with the Greek Orthodox and other Eastern churches was proclaimed in 1439. He also condemned the enslavement of the baptized people of the Canary Islands.

sections.h2: Canon of San Giorgio in Alga
paras: Gabriele Condulmer was born in Venice to a wealthy merchant family. As a young man he gave away much of his inheritance and joined a reform community of canons at San Giorgio in Alga. His uncle Gregory XII made him bishop of Siena and a cardinal in 1408.
Elected in March 1431, he immediately clashed with the Colonna, whose power had grown under Martin V, and with the Council of Basel, which opened that summer.

sections.h2: The Struggle with the Council of Basel
paras: Eugene tried to dissolve the Council of Basel in late 1431, but the council refused and reaffirmed Constance's claim that a general council holds authority even over the pope. Under pressure from Emperor Sigismund, whom he crowned in Rome in May 1433, and from much of Christendom, Eugene withdrew his dissolution later that year.

In 1434 a revolt in Rome forced him to flee the city by boat down the Tiber. He lived for most of the next nine years in Florence, where he consecrated the cathedral of Santa Maria del Fiore with its newly completed dome in 1436. Basel later declared him deposed and in 1439 elected the duke of Savoy as antipope Felix V, but few rulers followed.

sections.h2: Ferrara-Florence and Union with the East
paras: With the Byzantine Empire threatened by the Ottoman Turks, the emperor John VIII Palaiologos sought union with the West. Eugene transferred the council to Ferrara in 1438, where the Greek delegation joined it, and in 1439 moved it to Florence, partly because of plague.

On 6 July 1439 the decree Laetentur caeli proclaimed union between the Latin and Greek churches, affirming the procession of the Holy Spirit and the primacy of the Roman Pontiff. Union decrees with the Armenians and the Copts followed. The union with the Greeks was widely rejected in the East and did not survive the fall of Constantinople, but the council's decrees remained important in Catholic teaching. Eugene also supported the crusade that ended in defeat at Varna in 1444.

sections.h2: Sicut Dudum and the Canary Islands
paras: In the 1430s reports reached Eugene that Christian raiders were enslaving inhabitants of the Canary Islands, including those already baptized. In the bull Sicut dudum of January 1435, following earlier measures in 1434, he ordered that such captives be set free within a set time under penalty of excommunication.
Eugene returned to Rome in 1443 and died there on 23 February 1447. He had made peace with the German princes shortly before his death, a step toward the end of the Basel schism under his successor.

keyFacts: Born Gabriele Condulmer in Venice; nephew of Gregory XII
Canon regular of San Giorgio in Alga; cardinal from 1408
Transferred the council from Basel to Ferrara (1438) and Florence (1439)
Proclaimed union with the Greeks in Laetentur caeli (1439)
Condemned enslavement of baptized Canary Islanders in Sicut dudum (1435)

faqs.question: What was the Council of Florence?
faqs.answer: It was the general council Eugene IV moved from Basel to Ferrara in 1438 and then to Florence in 1439. There the Latin Church and the Byzantine delegation proclaimed reunion, though the union was later rejected in the East.

faqs.question: Why did Eugene IV live in Florence?
faqs.answer: A revolt in Rome in 1434 forced him to flee. He spent most of the following years in Florence, returning to Rome only in 1443.

faqs.question: What did Eugene IV say about slavery in the Canary Islands?
faqs.answer: In Sicut dudum (1435) he ordered that baptized Canary Islanders who had been enslaved be freed within a fixed period, on pain of excommunication for those who held them.
